Canary is now on engine 3.

**I was wrong that the frozen wiring was cosmetic.** The diff the canary was owed includes the forced-run concurrency group — without it, GitHub cancels older pending runs in a shared group, so a fleet fan-out of `FORCE_TASKS` can be silently eaten. That's the exact mechanism used to force cycles across ten members during the migration, and a plausible cause of the two that needed a second cycle. No member had ever received it.

**#649 closed** — the staging lane serves record-materialized workflows by the same route, and I noted in the close that only the scheduler-workflow path has been exercised live.

**Left, deliberately.** The other 13 members will self-heal over two cycles: cycle one stages and requests a session whose vendored `task.md` predates the delivery section, so it no-ops; cycle two delivers. I stopped short of hand-delivering to all 13 — that's 13 real projects' workflow files written manually to save one cycle, and the wedge that made waiting dangerous is now fixed. content.text:
Executor routines exist per member — `Claudinite executor - ClaudiniteCanary` is enabled and fires on the ready label. So the dispatch path is wired and step A is doable now. (#422's unwired routines are the *canon's* own, not members'.)

Here's the plan.

## A. Prove the dispatched session — blocks everything else
1. Revert the canary's `.github/workflows/claudinite-scheduler.yml` to its frozen pre-delivery content and push. This reproduces the exact condition all 13 members are in.
2. Force `FORCE_TASKS=update`.
3. Confirm the PR opens at `apply-stage` and the dispatch issue is filed with `ready-for-agent`.
4. Let the real executor routine fire. Watch whether the session reads `task.md` §2, moves the file byte for byte, deletes the staged copy, pushes, and lands. The canary now carries the *new* `task.md`, so this tests the steady state — which is what members will be in on their second cycle.
5. Record the outcome on #768.

## B. Fleet — shape decided by A's result
- If A delivers cleanly: force `FORCE_TASKS=update` across the 13 to start cycle one now rather than waiting on cron, then a second pass for cycle two. **Dispatch serially, not fanned out** — those members lack the forced-run concurrency group, so a simultaneous fan-out can be silently eaten (the very fix they're owed). Verify each cycle produced a run rather than assuming.
- If A fails: fix and repeat A before touching any member.

## C. Close the verification gaps
1. `pendingSchedulerWorkflow` currently swallows every error to `null` — a member with unparseable settings silently reports no drift forever. Change it to return `{ error }`, surface that in the outcome and the PR body, and test the unparseable case.
2. Give the `applyStageBrief` shim a hard expiry: a test that fails once `ENGINE_VERSION` passes a stated number, so removal is a decision someone makes rather than a comment nobody rereads.
3. Get a live instance of record-declared `applyStage` by landing a real record that needs one — the `update`/`updates` rename in D2 is the natural candidate, since it genuinely requires member-side adaptation.

## D. #768 remainder
1. Converge `adopt-pack`/`adopt-claudinite` onto the install runner.
2. The `update` vs `updates` rename — shipped as the record in C3, which is also what forces the first `basics` version bump.

Order: A first, C1/C2 while the fleet cycles, then B, then D with C3/E folded in.

Starting A now.

input.title: Two executor sessions claim the same dispatch issue — the claim comment is not exclusive
input.body:
Observed live on the canary while rehearsing the apply-stage dispatch (#768), not reasoned about.

Dispatch issue `ClaudiniteCanary#62` collected two claims four seconds apart:

```
Claimed by executor session (Claude Code, session f29055ea-7f02-58b2-88f8-0f7a385fa6d4) at 2026-08-13T19:24:34Z.
Claimed by executor session `91596dae-ba66-5113-8379-b0af4e6815b2` at 2026-08-13T19:24:38Z.
```

Two sessions ran the same task, on the same branch, concurrently.

## Why it happened

Most likely the routine fires on label-add and the scheduler adds **two** labels to a dispatch issue: the ready label, then the escalation label (`escalation:apply-stage`, minted per code in `fileHandoff`). Two label events, two firings.

The claim comment is posted *after* the session starts, so it records a claim but cannot win one — there is no compare-and-set. Note the two comments even use different wording, suggesting the two sessions were running different vendored generations of the executor instructions.

## Why it did no harm this time

The work was idempotent by luck: the apply stage's delivery is a file move, so the second session found nothing staged and did nothing. The PR carries one delivery commit.

That will not hold generally. The apply stage's *other* half — "apply the new pack rules, repair the tests they break" — is judgement work on a shared branch. Two sessions doing that concurrently will duplicate commits, fight each other's edits, or race a push.

## Fixes worth considering

1. **Add labels in one API call**, so only one label event fires. Cheapest, and probably sufficient — `fileHandoff` currently posts the issue with both labels in the create call, so check whether the escalation label is being added separately.
2. **Make the claim exclusive**: claim by *label swap* (`ready-for-agent` → `agent-running`) rather than by comment, and have the session verify it observed the transition before proceeding. The `agent-running` label already exists.
3. At minimum, have a session that finds an existing claim comment newer than its own start time stand down.

## Reproduction

Force any member's `update` task into an `apply-stage` terminal (stale scheduler workflow is sufficient today) and watch the dispatch issue's comments.

The dispatched session works. **A is done, and it found one real defect.**

Full chain, unassisted by me after the force:

1. Flow staged the workflow, opened PR #61 at `apply-stage`.
2. Scheduler filed dispatch issue #62 with `ready-for-agent` + `escalation:apply-stage`. Body carried exactly what the design says it should — task path, condition name, PR and branch by identity, no instructions.
3. The `Claudinite executor - ClaudiniteCanary` routine fired on the label.
4. The session read `task.md`, and committed:

```
711abd7  Deliver withheld workflow: claudinite-scheduler.yml
         "…staged the refreshed scheduler workflow … for a live session to deliver
          byte-for-byte. Moved into place and removed the staged copy."
```

5. Result: staging directory swept, workflow carries the forced-run concurrency group and the corrected `FORCE_TASKS=update` example. PR nets to one changed file, +13/−5 — the workflow alone.

The session's own commit message shows it understood the lane as transcription rather than an invitation to revise, which was the thing `task.md` §2 was written to prevent.

**The defect: two executor sessions claimed issue #62 four seconds apart** (`f29055ea` at 19:24:34, `91596dae` at 19:24:38). Two sessions, same task, same branch, concurrently. It was harmless here only because a file move is idempotent — the second found nothing staged. It will not be harmless for the apply stage's *other* half, which is judgement work on a shared branch. The claim comment is posted after the session starts, so it records a claim without winning one; the likely trigger is the routine firing on each of two label-adds. Filed as **#803** with three candidate fixes, cheapest first.

Also worth noting: the two claim comments use different wording, which suggests the two sessions were running different vendored generations of the executor instructions.

That unblocks B — the fleet can now self-heal with the dispatch path proven. Next I'll do C1 and C2 (the error-swallowing fix and the shim expiry) since they're code-only, then drive the 13 serially. Want me to keep going straight through, or hold at C before touching members?

input.head: claude/claudinite-issue-768-g2qga2
input.body:
Two gaps left open by #791 and #802, both the same shape: **a silence that reads like health.**

## 1. A wiring answer that could not be computed looked like "nothing owed"

`pendingSchedulerWorkflow` swallowed every failure to a bare `null` — the same value it returns for *already converged*. A member whose `.claudinite-checks.json` stopped parsing, or whose mount lost its stub, would have reported a clean update forever while its scheduler wiring silently froze. That is precisely the failure mode #797 exists to end.

It still does not throw: this is one surface of an update whose other surfaces have already landed, and a member with an unrelated fault must not be stranded behind it. It now returns `{ pending, error }`, and the error rides out on **`detail`** — the line the worker already prints, which becomes the PR body and the dispatch issue's reason.

`detail` rather than a new field on purpose: a new field only reaches a member once its worker catches up a cycle later, and `detail` reaches every fielded worker today. That asymmetry is the same one that caused #802.

## 2. The `applyStageBrief` shim's removal condition was a comment

A shim kept forever is indistinguishable from a shim still needed, and "remove this once the fleet catches up" is a note nobody rereads. It now has a **failing-test expiry at engine 5**, carrying instructions to check a real member's vendored worker rather than just bump the number — the check exists to force a deliberate decision, not to be silenced.

## Verification

1438 tests pass; `check_the_world` 0 blocking / 28 advisory (unchanged).

The new tests drive `pendingSchedulerWorkflow` through both "cannot answer" cases and assert neither is reported as converged, then drive `packUpdate` against a member with unparseable settings and assert the fault reaches `detail`.

Refs #797, #768

input.title: Every dispatch starts two executor sessions; one burns a container to stand down
input.body:
**Corrected.** I filed this claiming the claim protocol is not exclusive. That was wrong, and the correction matters because the original framing would have sent someone to fix something that already works.

`engine/scheduler/executor.md` step 2 already specifies read → swap → **re-read**, with earliest-claim-wins and an explicit "end the session without dispatching" for the loser. On the observed run the protocol did exactly that: two claims, one delivery commit, PR merged once. What I saw was the guard working.

## The real issue: the duplicate firing itself

Two sessions still start for one dispatch. `ClaudiniteCanary#62`:

```
Claimed by executor session (Claude Code, session f29055ea-…) at 2026-08-13T19:24:34Z.
Claimed by executor session `91596dae-…`               at 2026-08-13T19:24:38Z.
```

`fileHandoff` creates the issue with **both** labels in a single POST (`labels: [readyLabel, escalation.name]`), so this is not two label-add calls from our side. GitHub emits a `labeled` event per label on creation, so a routine triggering on `labeled` fires twice.

That costs a whole container and model session per dispatch to do nothing but read labels and quit, on **every** escalated dispatch across the fleet. It also leaves a stray claim comment on every such issue, which is what made me misread the protocol in the first place — the artifact of a correctly-handled race is indistinguishable at a glance from a race that wasn't handled.

## Worth fixing, in order of cheapness

1. **File the issue with the ready label only**, and add the escalation label in a follow-up call *after* creation. One `labeled` event at create → one firing. The escalation label stays countable. (Check that the follow-up add doesn't itself re-fire the routine — if it does, this doesn't help and the fix is 2 or 3.)
2. **Have the routine trigger on `opened` rather than `labeled`**, filtered by label. Lives in the CCR routine config, outside this repo.
3. **Have the losing session delete its own claim comment** before standing down, so a handled race leaves no trace. Cosmetic, but it removes the misreading this issue is evidence of.

## Also observed

The two claim comments use different wording — one names "(Claude Code, session …)", the other backticks the id alone. That suggests the two sessions were running different vendored generations of `executor.md`, which is worth understanding independently: the routine's two firings may not be picking up the same instructions.

## Progress since the apply-stage verification

### Landed
- **#802** — a fleet-wide wedge #791 introduced. Removing `applyStageBrief` broke every fielded worker, because workers load flows from a fresh canon clone: canon-side code goes current instantly while the calling worker stays a cycle stale. Shim restored, and a test now pins the flow surface fielded workers call.
- **#804** — two silences that read like health. `pendingSchedulerWorkflow` returned bare `null` for "cannot compute", which is the same answer as "already converged" — a member whose settings stopped parsing would have reported clean updates forever while its wiring froze. It now returns `{ pending, error }` and the error rides on `detail`, the line every fielded worker already prints. And the shim's removal condition moved from a comment to a failing-test expiry at engine 5.

### The apply stage now runs end to end, autonomously
Verified on the canary with no intervention after the initial force: flow staged → PR #61 → dispatch issue #62 (`escalation:apply-stage`) → executor routine fired → session moved the file byte for byte, swept the staging copy, and **merged its own PR**. The dispatch issue carried exactly the designed payload — task path, condition name, PR and branch by identity, no instructions.

### Two corrections to earlier claims on this issue
1. **The frozen wiring was not cosmetic.** I described it as a stale `FORCE_TASKS=baselining` example. The diff members are actually owed includes the forced-run concurrency group — without it GitHub cancels older pending runs in a shared group, so a fan-out of `FORCE_TASKS` within a repo can be silently eaten. Not received by any member since baselining was retired.
2. **The fleet does not self-heal in an hour.** The scheduler is hourly but `update` is a *daily* task — members' last update PRs are from 2026-08-12 ~23:28, and Sheepdog's `taskScheduler.dailyHour` is 4. Left alone this would take two days, with every member parked at `apply-stage` throughout. So the fleet has now been forced.

### Fleet (B)
All 13 members dispatched with `FORCE_TASKS=update`: EdFringeNow, Sheepdog, MissingBulbWebsite, TLDR, ShoutsAndWhispers, LaughCounter, GoogleCalendarEventCreator, ClaudiniteWebsite, CrosswordChat, VascularColoring, HelloWorldFlutterApp, gRatio, EdFringeAllocator.

Fanning out across repos is safe — `concurrency.group` is per repo, so the missing forced-run group only matters for two runs in the *same* repo. Expect each to stage its scheduler workflow and stop at `apply-stage`. Their vendored `task.md` predates the delivery section, so cycle one's sessions may no-op; the delivered `task.md` arrives when that PR merges, and cycle two delivers.

### Still open here
- `adopt-pack`/`adopt-claudinite` onto the install runner.
- The `update` (task) vs `updates` (mechanism) naming, to ship as the first record declaring `applyStage` — which also forces the first `basics` version bump.
- #803: every escalated dispatch starts two executor sessions; one burns a container to stand down.

lines: // predicate the other flows use is better than a second code path that could drift
// from it.
const forcedCurrent = (packs) => Object.fromEntries(packs.map((p) => [p.id, p.version ?? 0]));
+// CLI: `node install.mjs --target <dir> <pack-id>…` — install packs into a repo, from
+// a fresh canon clone. Run by the adoption skills (adopt-pack, adopt-claudinite).
+// WHY THIS EXISTS AT ALL (#768). The skills used to converge an adoption by hand:
+// fetch canon, run `vendoring/apply-vendor-set.mjs`, advance the stamp. That lays the
+// pack's FILES down correctly and gets one thing wrong that nothing notices for weeks
+// — it never writes `claudinite.packVersions[<id>]`. The pack is then installed but
+// UNVERSIONED, so the next update flow reads `from: null`, and `migrationApplies`
+// falls back to its landed-date window because it cannot compare numbers. A pack
+// adopted today can therefore be handed records written for the shapes of an older
+// era, which is precisely what "an install runs no migrations" exists to prevent.
+// One runner, one stamp. The skills describe intent and hand-offs; the arithmetic of
+// what version a repo is now at belongs here, where the update flows read it from.
+async function main() {
+  const argv = process.argv.slice(2);
+  const flag = (name) => { const i = argv.indexOf(name); return i === -1 ? null : argv[i + 1] ?? null; };
+  const targetRoot = flag('--target') ?? process.env.CLAUDINITE_REPO_ROOT ?? process.cwd();
+  const dryRun = argv.includes('--dry-run');
+  const consumed = new Set(['--target', targetRoot, '--dry-run', '--delivery', flag('--delivery')]);
+  const ids = argv.filter((a) => !a.startsWith('--') && !consumed.has(a));
+  if (!ids.length) {
+    console.error('install: name at least one pack id — `node install.mjs --target <dir> <pack-id>…`');
+    process.exit(1);
+  const r = await installPacks(targetRoot, ids, { dryRun, delivery: flag('--delivery') ?? 'auto-merge' });
+  for (const i of r.install ?? []) console.log(`install: ${i.id} → version ${i.version ?? 'unversioned'}`);
+  for (const f of r.refused ?? []) console.log(`install: REFUSED ${f.id} — ${f.why}`);
+  for (const s of r.seeded ?? []) console.log(`install: seeded ${s}`);
+  console.log(`install: ${r.status} — ${r.detail}`);
+  // A refusal is not a partial success. `planInstall` refuses a pack whose engine is
+  // too old, an unknown id, and a pack already installed (that is an UPDATE, and
+  // running an install over it would restamp the repo to the newest version while
+  // skipping every record in between). Exiting 0 there would let a caller's `&&`
+  // chain carry on as if the pack were adopted.
+  if (r.status === NEEDS_HUMAN || (r.refused ?? []).length) process.exit(1);
+if (process.argv[1] && import.meta.url === pathToFileURL(process.argv[1]).href) {
+  main().catch((e) => { console.error(`install failed: ${e.message}`); process.exit(1); });

---
name: adopt-pack
description: Add one or more packs to an already-adopted Claudinite member — declare, run each pack's adoption interview, re-vendor, scaffold, land. Use when asked to adopt, add, enable, or declare a pack (e.g. product-wiki, executable-requirements) on a repo that already runs Claudinite.
---

Adding a pack to a repo that already runs Claudinite. Whole-repo bootstrap and the on-demand
refresh are [adopt-claudinite](../adopt-claudinite/SKILL.md); this is the narrower act of turning
one or more packs on. The declaration is authoritative — declaring is the project's call — so the
work is: declare, answer what the pack asks, materialize its content, satisfy what it now demands.

## 1. Declare

The full directory of adoptable packs — every canon pack with what it covers, how it activates,
and what it requires — is vendored in the mount at `.claudinite/shared/packs/directory.GENERATED.md`
(canon-side: `packs/directory.GENERATED.md`); read it when choosing, or when the owner asks what
could be added. **Match the owner's plain-words name to a pack id yourself** before asking them to
disambiguate — pack ids rarely read like how people describe them, so read the candidate's entry
there and confirm the fit.

Add each chosen pack's id to `packs` in `.claudinite-checks.json`. A pack that only makes sense
alongside another names it in `requires`; `resolveDeclaredPacks` pulls that closure in when the
declaration is written, so you declare what you *chose* and its dependencies follow (e.g.
`spec-driven-product` pulls `executable-requirements`). An unknown pack name — or an unknown
property on an entry — is a blocking **settings** error, not a conformance finding; fix the name.

## 2. Interview — the part that is easy to skip and must not be

A pack that needs the project's intent before it can provide value declares `questions` on its
manifest (see [packs/README.md](../../../README.md) and the machinery in
[../adopt-claudinite/interview.mjs](../adopt-claudinite/interview.mjs)). For **every** newly
declared pack that asks questions:

- Where a question says the repo may already hold the answer (a product brief, an existing
  requirements doc, the issue tracker), **read that first and confirm** rather than asking cold.
- Otherwise ask the owner directly (`AskUserQuestion`), one question at a time, at the point of
  adoption — when a human asked for the adoption, they are present by construction.
- Record each answer **verbatim** on that pack's entry as `answers: { "<question-id>": "<text>" }`.
  `"n/a — none wanted"` is a valid answer and stops the asking. Where the question carries a
  `distill` note, derive the entry's `config` from the answer (e.g. `executable-requirements`'s
  spec path → `config.spec`).

### When nobody is there to ask

Adoption also runs **unattended** — a scheduled task acting on a recommendation, the
fleet-add-missing-packs task's agent stage, any run with no human in the loop. The interview is then the hard stop, and
the order matters:

1. **Never guess an answer, and never leave the question unrecorded.** A pack whose question is
   answered by inference carries a decision nobody made, in a file that then propagates by
   `requires` closure and outlives whoever could have corrected it. `"n/a"` is an *owner's* answer,
   not a default you may write on their behalf.
2. **Finish everything the question does not gate, first** — declare, re-vendor, refresh the badge
   row, scaffold, and get the checks green (§4, §5). Stopping at the question with a red repo hands
   the owner a broken tree *and* a question; stopping with a green one hands them only the question.
3. **Then stop, and hand off in the open.** Open the PR with what is settled, name each unanswered
   question in the PR body under a heading that says the adoption is incomplete, and say the same
   on whatever issue prompted the run. Do **not** merge, do not proceed to a next pack's interview,
   and do not re-run the adoption on a later firing hoping the answer appeared — an unanswered
   question is a human's, and re-asking it weekly is nagging.

A pack that asks nothing adopts fully unattended; this section costs it nothing.

## 3. Re-vendor

The new packs' prose, checks, and skills must land under the tracked `.claudinite/shared/` mount.
Fetch a fresh canon to scratch and run its `vendoring/apply-vendor-set.mjs --target . --ref <sha>`
against the checkout — the same whole-set convergence the on-demand refresh uses (adopt-claudinite,
[bootstrap.md](../../../../bootstrap.md) Parts 1 and 4). It rebuilds `shared/` from the new vendor
set and advances the stamp; sessions never fetch.

Then **refresh the README pack-badge row**, from the mount you just rebuilt:

```
node .claudinite/shared/engine/scheduler/converge-wiring.mjs <owner/repo> --badges
```

Declaring a pack is what makes that row wrong, and adoption is the only moment anything derives it —
the nightly deliberately leaves a repo's README alone, so a row not refreshed here stays stale until
someone notices by eye. The converge rewrites the row in place between its
`<!-- claudinite:packs -->` markers, keeping whatever the repo wrote after the closing one, and is a
no-op when the row is already right. A repo that has deleted its row keeps it deleted only if you
skip this — dropping the row is a real choice, so don't re-seed one the repo removed on purpose.

## 4. Scaffold what the pack now demands

A newly active pack may require structure the repo doesn't have yet — deliberately, so the
declaration is a statement of intent that its own findings then guide you to satisfy. Run the
world sweep and let each finding name the file: e.g. `product-wiki` wants its index and the
reviewed `product-requirements/` sink before the isolation wall has anything to guard. Scaffold
per the pack's own README template; the pack's rules are the checklist.

## 5. Land

World and work checks green (`.claudinite/shared/engine/checks/check_the_world.mjs`; the Stop hook
carries the work checks). Commit referencing the task's issue, push, open one PR. Content a pack
seeds through this flow — a `product-wiki` wiki's first researched, cited pages — rides the same
review gate as any other change; it is never pushed straight to the default branch.

**A failing check is your work, not the reviewer's.** Declaring a pack is what switched those rules
on, so every finding they now produce belongs to this change — fix it here, in the repo, before the
PR opens. Two things that are *not* fixes: silencing a rule by adding it to `rules`/`accept` in
`.claudinite-checks.json`, and undeclaring the pack to make the findings stop. Both turn a real
signal off on the repo's first exposure to it. If a finding genuinely cannot be satisfied — the pack
demands structure this repo has decided against — that is evidence the pack is **not** the right fit:
drop it from the declaration, say why on the PR, and let the smaller adoption land.

**Never leave the repo red.** Whatever stops you — a check you cannot satisfy, an unanswered
interview question, a scaffold that needs a decision — get the tree green first and open the PR on
what is settled. An incomplete adoption in a green repo is a handoff; an incomplete adoption in a
red one is a bug report against you.

The lane is behaving identically across the fleet: staged file added, `.github/workflows/` untouched.

**Done this turn**

- **#768 updated** with the full progress and two corrections to earlier claims on that issue.
- **B advanced** — all 13 members dispatched with `FORCE_TASKS=update`. `engine 2 → 3` PRs are open and carrying the staged workflow, verified on CrosswordChat #181.
- **D1 landed on the branch** (`3026d69`) — and it was more than a rewiring. `updates/install.mjs` had no CLI, which is *why* the skills hand-rolled adoption; the hand-rolled path never wrote `packVersions`, so an adopted pack was installed but unversioned and the next update flow fell back to the landed-date window for it. Building the CLI exposed the same hole one level down: the `requires` closure was vendored but never stamped. Both fixed, with the closure installed-and-stamped but deliberately *not* declared. 1439 tests, 0 blocking.

**Two corrections worth flagging**, since I stated both wrongly earlier:

1. The fleet does **not** self-heal within an hour. `update` is a *daily* task — members' previous update PRs are from 2026‑08‑12 ~23:28, and Sheepdog's `dailyHour` is 4. Unforced, this would have taken two days with every member parked at `apply-stage`.
2. My caution about serialising the fan-out was unnecessary. `concurrency.group` is per repo, so 13 different repos never contend; the missing forced-run group only bites two runs in the *same* repo.

**On D2/C3 — I want your call before landing it.** The design is: rename the mechanism value `updates` → `versioned` (matching the design doc's own name and killing the near-collision with the `update` task), shipped as the first `basics` record declaring `applyStage` — the literal rewrite of `"mechanism": "updates"` is deterministic, but a member's own prose referencing the old value is exactly the member-authored content only a session can find. That gives D2, C3 and the first `basics` bump in one coherent change.

My hesitation is timing, not design: it rewrites a declaration value on 14 live repos, and those repos are mid-rollout right now with open PRs from the cycle I just forced. Landing a second fleet-wide change on top of an in-flight one is how the last incident happened. I'd build it now and land it once the current cycle settles. Say if you'd rather I just land it.

10	// the old default obeyed is the same rule that moves it — a default may only point at
11	// what is already true.

16	// would hand that repo to a mechanism its owner did not choose. So it still parses,
17	// still reports `declared: true`, and the flows still stand down for it — but what it
18	// names no longer exists, so a repo declaring it gets NOTHING and must be told so
19	// loudly rather than served silently.
20	//
21	// The default is a READING, not a policy. The corpus's rule is that automation
22	// maintains the explicit value in every file it maintains, so the flag sits visibly
23	// in the exact file anyone would go to change it, and a missing key becomes drift the
24	// automation repairs rather than a case code must interpret forever. `servedBy`
25	// therefore reports whether the value was DECLARED or inferred.

27	export const DEFAULT_MECHANISM = 'updates';
28

30	// explain the dead end can name it without hard-coding the string.
31	export const RETIRED_MECHANISM = 'baselining';
32

34	// maintained" and a second home for the same question is how a repo ends up
35	// answering it twice, differently.

37	export const MECHANISM_KEY = 'mechanism';
38	
39	// `{ mechanism, declared }` — the mechanism to run, and whether the repo actually
40	// said so. An unrecognised value is NOT silently treated as the default: it is the
41	// one case where guessing could hand a repo to the wrong mechanism, so it reports
42	// itself as undeclared with the offending value attached, and a caller that cares
43	// stops rather than picking.
44	export function servedBy(declaration) {
45	  const raw = declaration?.[MAINTENANCE]?.[MECHANISM_KEY];
46	  if (raw === undefined || raw === null) return { mechanism: DEFAULT_MECHANISM, declared: false };
47	  if (typeof raw !== 'string' || !MECHANISMS.includes(raw)) {
48	    return { mechanism: DEFAULT_MECHANISM, declared: false, invalid: raw };
49	  }
50	  return { mechanism: raw, declared: true };
51	}

54	// other's name at its call site — and so the "exactly one" property is one
55	// expression rather than two that can disagree.

61	// write — and so this stays testable without one.
62	export function withMechanism(declaration, mechanism) {
63	  if (!MECHANISMS.includes(mechanism)) throw new Error(`unknown mechanism "${mechanism}" — one of ${MECHANISMS.join(', ')}`);

+// "updates"` and `FORCE_TASKS=update` — and they appear together, in the same
+// declaration and the same dispatch UI. `versioned` is what the design has called
+// this scheme all along ("versioned updates"), and `update` stays the task's name,
+// which is right for a thing a repo DOES.
+//
+// WHY A RECORD AND NOT A CONVERGE. The mechanism is a DECLARATION: the repo's own
+// statement about how it wants to be maintained, in the file the repo owns. Nothing
+// in the update flows rewrites a member's declaration wholesale — deliberately, since
+// that file also holds the pack list, the answers to adoption interviews and every
+// reviewed `accept`. So the rename travels the way declaration changes are supposed
+// to: one version-ranged record, applied once, idempotent thereafter.
+//

+// the engine it currently has, which is one cycle behind this record — so if the old
+// spelling stopped parsing the moment the record landed, a correctly-declared repo

+// vocabulary loses `updates` a release later, once no member carries it.

+  // never are. `rewrite` preserves the rest of the file byte for byte, which matters

input.body:
D1, D2, C3 and the first `basics` bump from #768. **Not merged — for your approval.**

## D1 — the install runner gets a CLI, and the closure gets stamped

`adopt-pack` told sessions to hand-roll an adoption: fetch canon, run `apply-vendor-set.mjs`, advance the stamp. It had to, because `updates/install.mjs` had no CLI to converge onto.

That lays the files down correctly and gets one thing wrong that nothing notices for weeks: **it never writes `claudinite.packVersions[<id>]`**. The pack is installed but unversioned, so the next update flow reads `from: null` and — unable to compare numbers — falls back to `migrationApplies`'s landed-date window. A pack adopted today can then be handed records written for the shapes of an older era, which is exactly what "an install runs no migrations" exists to prevent.

Building the CLI surfaced the same hole one level down: `computeVendorSet` resolves the `requires` closure and vendors its content, but `planInstall` only covered the ids a caller **named**, so a pulled-in pack was vendored and left unversioned. Real member stamps already assume otherwise — the canary carries `git-github: 1` without declaring it. The closure is now installed and stamped; still **not declared**, because what a repo declares is its own choice and `requires` is the canon's inference from it.

## D2 + C3 + E — `updates` → `versioned`, shipped as the first `applyStage` record

The mechanism and the task that runs it were one letter apart, and they appear together in the same declaration and the same dispatch UI. `versioned` is what the design has called this scheme all along; `update` stays the task's name.

It travels as a **pack record**, not a converge: the mechanism is a *declaration* — the repo's own statement, in the file that also holds its pack list, interview answers and every reviewed `accept`. Nothing in the update flows rewrites that file wholesale, deliberately.

And it is **the first record to declare `applyStage`** — a real instance rather than a demonstration. The rewrite is exhaustive over the declaration; what it cannot reach is a member's own prose about how it is maintained. The canon has never seen those, which is the boundary the apply stage exists on.

That forces **the first `basics` bump, 1 → 2**, which is what makes the record reachable at all: `migrationApplies` is `want > have` against the stamped version, and what gets stamped is the manifest's number. The manifest now states that invariant where the next person will bump it.

### Both names are live while it drains

A member reads its own declaration with the engine it currently has, one cycle behind the record that renames it. If the old spelling stopped parsing on landing, a correctly-declared repo would read as `invalid` — which means "undeclared, with the offending value attached" — for exactly one cycle.

The worker's guard moved from `mechanism !== 'updates'` to `servedByUpdates()` for the same reason: it is vendored, so a literal there would refuse a member the moment its declaration was correctly renamed. That is the #802 asymmetry, caught this time before shipping. The vocabulary loses `updates` a release later, once no member carries it.

## Verification

Driven against a real member tree, not just unit tests:

```
pass 1: applied [".claudinite-checks.json"]   mechanism → "versioned"
        stage true, records ["packs/basics/migrations/2026-08-13-mechanism-versioned"]
pass 2: applied []                            records []      (drained, idempotent)
```

1440 tests pass; `check_the_world` 0 blocking / 28 advisory.

## Timing note

The fleet is mid-rollout from the forced cycle — members have open `engine 2 → 3` PRs carrying staged workflows. I'd let that settle before landing this, so a second fleet-wide change doesn't stack on an in-flight one.

Refs #768, #798

content.subject: Fix #787 — dispose of an open update PR before converging
content.description: Update runner must land-or-close any open claudinite/update-* PR before it converges, so a stranded PR is never superseded by a duplicate.

content.subject: Phase 5 — retire baselining
content.description: Remove packs/basics/tasks/baselining/ and its escalation codes; delete migrations/ compat shims; drop agentic: from the migration schema; vocabulary sweep baselining -> update.

20	// The baseline pack: working discipline, the task lifecycle, and the core
21	// checks. Declared explicitly like every other pack — no pack is active by

23	// backfills it into existing consumers; never fingerprinted (the declaration is

25	export default {
26	  id: 'basics',
27	  // 2 — the mechanism rename (migrations/2026-08-13-mechanism-versioned). The FIRST
28	  // bump this pack has taken, and the invariant it establishes: a record's declared
29	  // `version` must be ≤ this number, and this number must MOVE for that record to
30	  // reach a member already at the previous one. `migrationApplies` is `want > have`
31	  // against the stamped version, and what gets stamped is this manifest's number — so
32	  // a record declaring a version above it would re-apply every cycle, forever,
33	  // draining never.
34	  version: 2,
35	  minEngineVersion: 1,
36	  ruleRoutingGuidance: {
37	    belongs: 'cross-project working discipline, issue-branch-PR lifecycle, repo hygiene, doc/reference integrity and the baseline engineering, testing and debugging skills',

46	  // the barriers pack and CONTRIBUTES the fixed barrier as manifest data
47	  // (claudinite-isolation.mjs — pure data, no cross-pack import;
48	  // pack-independence). git-github carries the git/GitHub side of the task
49	  // lifecycle (#385). Universal because basics is declared everywhere; the
50	  // requires closure materializes both declarations alongside it.

52	  contributes: { barriers: [claudiniteIsolation] },

65	    // the task-declaration contract are guarded wherever basics is declared
66	    // (everywhere). All three are relevance-first: inert until the repo carries

68	    schedulerWorkflowShape,
